modules.title: Module 1: Hindi Script Fundamentals & Unicode Basics
modules.content:
## The Devanagari Script at a Glance  

Imagine you need to type a quick thank‑you note to a friend in Hindi: “धन्यवाद, मित्र!” You reach for the keyboard, press a few keys, and the screen instantly shows the beautiful Devanagari characters. If the letters appear as random boxes or Latin symbols instead, the message is lost. The reason lies in how the script is stored and rendered by computers – a topic we’ll unpack from the ground up.

### What is Devanagari?  
Devanagari (देवनागरी) is the writing system used for Hindi, Marathi, Sanskrit, and several other Indian languages. It is an **abugida**, meaning each consonant carries an inherent vowel sound (usually “अ” /ə/). Vowels can appear **independently** (as stand‑alone letters) or as **matras** that attach to a consonant to modify its vowel sound.

### The Building Blocks  

| Category | Role in the script | Number in Hindi (standard) |
|----------|-------------------|----------------------------|
| **Vowels (स्वर)** | Represent pure vowel sounds; also provide the matras that modify consonants. | 13 independent letters |
| **Consonants (व्यंजन)** | Form the skeleton of words; each carries an implicit “अ”. | 33 basic letters |
| **Matras (मात्रा)** | Diacritic marks that replace the implicit “अ” on a consonant, yielding a different vowel sound. | 13 primary signs (including the “null” matra) |

The script also contains a handful of **special signs** – the halant (्) that suppresses the inherent vowel, the anusvara (ं) for nasalization, and the visarga (ः) for a breathy sound – but the three categories above are the core focus for anyone beginning to type Hindi.

---

## Mapping Devanagari to Unicode  

### Why Unicode matters  
Computers store text as numbers. Early computer systems used separate code pages for each language (e.g., ASCII for English, ISO‑8859‑1 for many European languages). This fragmented approach caused **garbled text** when a document moved between systems that spoke different “code languages.”  

**Unicode** is a universal standard that assigns a unique number, called a **code point**, to every character used in the world’s writing systems. When you type a Hindi character, the operating system looks up its Unicode code point and stores that number. Any modern device that understands Unicode can then retrieve the same character, regardless of the underlying hardware or software.

### How each Devanagari character gets a code point  

| Type | Unicode block | Range (hex) |
|------|----------------|-------------|
| **Devanagari letters** | U+0900 – U+097F | 0900‑097F |
| **Vowel letters** | U+0904 – U+0914 | 0904 (अ) … 0914 (औ) |
| **Consonant letters** | U+0915 – U+0939 | 0915 (क) … 0939 (ह) |
| **Matras (vowel signs)** | U+093A – U+094C | 093A (ॲ) … 094C (ौ) |
| **Halant (virama)** | U+094D | 094D (्) |
| **Anusvara, Visarga, Chandrabindu** | U+0900 – U+0903 | 0900 (ॐ) … 0903 (ः) |

For example, the word **“भारत”** (Bharat) is stored as the sequence:  

1. **भ** – U+092D  
2. **ा** – U+093E (matra for “ा”)  
3. **र** – U+0930  
4. **त** – U+0924  

When a Unicode‑aware application renders these code points, it automatically places the matra “ा” to the right of **भ**, producing the visual form “भा”.

### A concrete scenario  

You copy the Hindi phrase “सुप्रभात” from a web page and paste it into an old word processor that only supports the legacy “Windows‑1252” code page. The result appears as “? ? ? ? ?”. The underlying issue is that the program cannot interpret the Unicode code points (U+0938, U+094D, etc.) and falls back to placeholder characters. Installing a Unicode‑compatible font or switching the document’s encoding instantly resolves the problem, underscoring why Unicode is the backbone of modern Hindi typing.

---

## Independent Letters vs. Combined Forms  

### Independent (stand‑alone) letters  
When a vowel appears at the beginning of a word or after a space, it is written as an **independent letter**. For instance, the word **“अगला”** starts with the vowel “अ” (U+0905). Independent letters occupy a full character width and are stored as a single Unicode code point.

### Combined forms (conjuncts)  
When two or more consonants occur together without an intervening vowel, Devanagari creates a **conjunct** (also called a **ligature**). The most common way to form a conjunct is to place a **halant** (्, U+094D) after the first consonant, signalling that its inherent “अ” should be suppressed.  

Example: **“क्ष”** (kṣa) is a combination of **क** (U+0915) + **्** (U+094D) + **ष** (U+0937). The rendering engine may replace this three‑code‑point sequence with a single glyph that looks like a fused “kṣ” shape.

While this chapter does not dive deeply into the many possible conjuncts, recognizing the pattern “consonant + halant + next consonant” will help you spot combined forms as you type.

---

## Vowel Signs (Matras) – How They Transform Consonants  

### The five basic vowel signs  

| Vowel | Independent letter | Matra (sign) | Unicode | Placement |
|-------|--------------------|--------------|---------|-----------|
| अ (a) | अ | — (no sign) | U+0905 | No visual change – the inherent vowel |
| आ (ā) | आ | ा | U+093E | To the **right** of the consonant |
| इ (i) | इ | ि | U+093F | To the **left** of the consonant |
| ई (ī) | ई | ी | U+0940 | To the **right** of the consonant |
| उ (u) | उ | ि? (actually ु) | U+0941 | **Below** the consonant |
| ऊ (ū) | ऊ | ू | U+0942 | **Below** the consonant |
| ए (e) | ए | े | U+0947 | To the **right** of the consonant |
| ऐ (ai) | ऐ |ै | U+0948 | To the **right** of the consonant |
| ओ (o) | ओ | ो | U+094B | To the **right** of the consonant |
| औ (au) | औ | ौ | U+094C | To the **right** of the consonant |

> **Note:** The “null” matra (no sign) represents the inherent “अ”. When you type a consonant without adding any vowel sign, the system automatically assumes this vowel.

### Placement rules  

1. **Left‑side matras** (e.g., ि) appear *before* the consonant glyph but are stored **after** it in the Unicode stream.  
2. **Right‑side matras** (e.g., ा, ी, े) appear *after* the consonant glyph.  
3. **Below‑side matras** (e.g., ु, ू) sit beneath the consonant.  
4. **Above‑side matras** are rare in modern Hindi but exist for certain Sanskrit loanwords.

The rendering engine reorders the visual placement based on the type of matra; you never need to type the sign in a different order.

### Example transformations  

| Base consonant | No matra (inherent “अ”) | With “ा” (ā) | With “ि” (i) | With “ु” (u) |
|----------------|------------------------|--------------|--------------|--------------|
| क (ka) | क | **का** (kā) – क + ा | **कि** (ki) – क + ि | **कु** (ku) – क + ु |
| म (ma) | म | **मा** (mā) – म + ा | **मि** (mi) – म + ि | **मु** (mu) – म + ु |

Notice how the visual shape of the consonant stays the same; only the attached matra changes the spoken vowel.

---

## Quick Reference Tables  

### Vowels – Independent Forms and Matras  

| Independent Letter | Unicode | Matra | Unicode | Example (with क) |
|---------------------|---------|-------|---------|------------------|
| अ | U+0905 | — | — | क |
| आ | U+0906 | ा | U+093E | **का** |
| इ | U+0907 | ि | U+093F | **कि** |
| ई | U+0908 | ी | U+0940 | **की** |
| उ | U+0909 | ु | U+0941 | **कु** |
| ऊ | U+090A | ू | U+0942 | **कू** |
| ए | U+090F | े | U+0947 | **के** |
| ऐ | U+0910 |ै | U+0948 | **कै** |
| ओ | U+0913 | ो | U+094B | **को** |
| औ | U+0914 | ौ | U+094C | **कौ** |

### Consonants – Core Set  

| Consonant | Unicode | Typical Transliteration |
|-----------|---------|------------------------|
| क | U+0915 | k |
| ख | U+0916 | kh |
| ग | U+0917 | g |
| घ | U+0918 | gh |
| ङ | U+0919 | ṅ |
| च | U+091A | c |
| छ | U+091B | ch |
| ज | U+091C | j |
| झ | U+091D | jh |
| ञ | U+091E | ñ |
| ट | U+091F | ṭ |
| ठ | U+0920 | ṭh |
| ड | U+0921 | ḍ |
| ढ | U+0922 | ḍh |
| ण | U+0923 | ṇ |
| त | U+0924 | t |
| थ | U+0925 | th |
| द | U+0926 | d |
| ध | U+0927 | dh |
| न | U+0928 | n |
| प | U+092A | p |
| फ | U+092B | ph |
| ब | U+092C | b |
| भ | U+092D | bh |
| म | U+092E | m |
| य | U+092F | y |
| र | U+0930 | r |
| ल | U+0932 | l |
| व | U+0935 | v |
| श | U+0936 | sh |
| ष | U+0937 | ṣ |
| स | U+0938 | s |
| ह | U+0939 | h |

### Common Vowel Sign Combinations  

| Consonant + Matra | Resulting Syllable | Unicode Sequence (hex) |
|-------------------|-------------------|------------------------|
| क + ा | का | 0915 093E |
| क + ि | क़ (visually “कि”) | 0915 093F |
| क + ी | की | 0915 0940 |
| क + ु | कु | 0915 0941 |
| क + ू | कू | 0915 0942 |
| क + े | के | 0915 0947 |
| क + ै | कै | 0915 0948 |
| क + ो | को | 0915 094B |
| क + ौ | कौ | 0915 094C |

These tables act as a cheat‑sheet when you begin typing. Memorizing the Unicode ranges is not required; modern input methods handle the mapping for you. However, knowing the code point layout helps when troubleshooting garbled text or when working with plain‑text files that expose raw Unicode values.

---

## From Script to Screen – A Mini‑Workflow  

1. **Press a key** on an Hindi‑enabled keyboard layout.  
2. The operating system **looks up** the corresponding Unicode code point (e.g., pressing “k” on an Inscript layout yields U+0915).  
3. The **font engine** retrieves the glyph for that code point from a Devanagari‑compatible font (such as *Mangal* or *Noto Sans Devanagari*).  
4. If a **matra** follows, the engine repositions the glyph according to the matra’s placement rule, producing the final visual syllable.  
5. The **Unicode string** (a series of code points) is stored in the document, ensuring that any device that reads the file can reconstruct the same visual representation.

Understanding this pipeline demystifies why a missing font or an outdated encoding can turn “धन्यवाद” into “?????” on another computer.

---

## Practice Corner – Spot the Pattern  

Below are five Hindi words. Identify the **independent vowel**, the **consonant base**, and the **matra** (if any). Write the Unicode sequence in hex for each word.

1. **आशा**  
2. **ग्राम**  
3. **सूर्य**  
4. **पुस्तक**  
5. **भोजन**

*Solution Sketch* (not included in the main text):  

1. आ (U+0906) – independent vowel; श (U+0936) + ा (U+093E) → 0906 0936 093E  
2. ग (U+0917) + र (U+0930) + ा (U+093E) + म (U+092E) → 0917 0930 093E 092E  
3. स (U+0938) + ू (U+0942) + र (U+0930) + य (U+092F) → 0938 0942 0930 092F  
4. प (U+092A) + ु (U+0941) + स् (स+्) → 092A 0941 0938 094D 0924 0915  
5. भ (U+092D) + ो (U+094B) + ज (U+091C) + न (U+0928) → 092D 094B 091C 0928  

Working through such exercises strengthens the mental link between visual forms and their underlying Unicode representation.

---

## Key Takeaways  

- **Devanagari** is an abugida where each consonant carries an inherent “अ” unless a **matra** replaces it.  
- **Vowels** appear either as **independent letters** (at word‑initial positions) or as **matras** attached to consonants.  
- **Unicode** assigns a unique code point to every Devanagari character, enabling consistent storage and rendering across devices.  
- The **halant (्)** suppresses the inherent vowel and signals the formation of **conjuncts** (combined consonant forms).  
- **Matras** modify consonants by appearing left, right, above, or below the base glyph; the visual placement is handled automatically by the rendering engine.  
- Knowing the basic Unicode ranges (U+0900‑U+097F) and the common vowel‑sign mappings equips you to diagnose encoding problems and to type Hindi confidently.  

With these foundations, you are ready to move on to installing and configuring Hindi input methods, where the concepts of script structure and Unicode will translate directly into practical typing skills.

modules.content:
## Why Enable Hindi Input?  

Imagine you are drafting a thank‑you email to a professor who teaches you in Hindi. You type the greeting “नमस्ते प्रोफेसर,” but the letters appear as garbled symbols like “ÃÂÃÂÃÂâ€¦”. The cause is simple: your computer is still set to an English keyboard layout, and the Devanagari characters you entered are being interpreted using the wrong encoding. By activating a Hindi input method, you tell the operating system to treat keystrokes as **Unicode** code points that map to the Devanagari letters you learned in Module 1 (e.g., “अ” U+0905, “क” U+0915). Once the language support is in place, the text appears correctly, and you can focus on expressing ideas rather than fixing broken characters.

---

## Understanding Keyboard Layouts  

A **keyboard layout** is a map that tells the computer which Unicode code point to generate for each physical key press. For Hindi, two popular families are:

| Layout | How it works | Typical users |
|--------|--------------|---------------|
| **Inscript** | Places every Devanagari letter, matra, and special sign on a dedicated key, following the official Indian government standard. | Learners who want a systematic, one‑to‑one mapping and who plan to type fast once memorized. |
| **Phonetic (Transliteration)** | Lets you type Hindi by approximating the sound of each letter using the Roman alphabet (e.g., typing “namaste” produces “नमस्ते”). | Users who are comfortable with English typing and need a gentle transition. |

Both layouts rely on an **Input Method Editor (IME)** – a small program that sits between the keyboard and the application, converting keystrokes into the appropriate Unicode characters. The IME is what you will install and configure on Windows and macOS.

---

## Enabling Hindi on Windows 10/11  

### 1. Add Hindi as a language  

1. Open **Settings** (Windows + I).  
2. Click **Time & language** → **Language & region**.  
3. Under **Preferred languages**, click **Add a language**.  
4. In the search box type **Hindi** and select **हिन्दी (India)**, then click **Next**.  
5. Keep the default options (install language pack, set as display language – optional) and click **Install**.  

> **Tip:** The installation may take a minute while Windows downloads the necessary language files.

### 2. Install the desired keyboard layout  

1. Still in **Language & region**, locate **हिन्दी (India)** in the list and click **Options**.  
2. Under **Keyboards**, click **Add a keyboard**.  
3. Choose one of the following:  
   * **Hindi – INSCRIPT** – the standard layout.  
   * **Hindi – Phonetic** – often listed as **Hindi (Transliteration)** or provided by third‑party IMEs such as **Google Input Tools**.  

   *If you prefer a third‑party phonetic IME:*  
   * Download the installer from the vendor’s website (e.g., Google Input Tools).  
   * Run the installer and follow the on‑screen prompts; it will add a new entry under **Keyboards**.

### 3. Verify the layout is active  

1. Click the **language icon** (ENG, HIN, etc.) on the taskbar.  
2. Select **हिन्दी (India) – INSCRIPT** (or the phonetic option).  
3. Open **Notepad** and type a few characters:  
   * For INSCRIPT, press **Shift + k** to get “क”.  
   * For phonetic, type “ka” and watch it convert to “क”.  

If the characters display correctly, the IME is functioning.

### 4. Set up a quick switch shortcut  

Windows provides two built‑in shortcuts:  

* **Windows + Space** – cycles through all installed input languages.  
* **Left Alt + Shift** – switches between the current language’s keyboards (e.g., INSCRIPT ↔ Phonetic).  

You can customize them:  

1. Open **Settings** → **Devices** → **Typing** → **Advanced keyboard settings**.  
2. Click **Input language hotkeys** → **Change language bar hot keys**.  
3. Choose **Between input languages** and click **Change Key Sequence** to assign your preferred combination.

---

## Enabling Hindi on macOS (Ventura and later)

### 1. Add Hindi to the system language list  

1. Open **System Settings** ( → System Settings).  
2. Navigate to **Keyboard** → **Input Sources**.  
3. Click the **+** button below the list of input sources.  

### 2. Choose a Hindi keyboard  

In the **Add an Input Source** dialog:  

* **Hindi – Devanagari (INSCRIPT)** – the official layout.  
* **Hindi – Transliteration** – provided by Apple’s built‑in phonetic option.  

Select the desired layout and click **Add**. The new source appears in the left‑hand column.

### 3. Activate the keyboard  

1. Ensure the checkbox next to the newly added Hindi source is ticked.  
2. Close the settings window.  

### 4. Switch between languages  

* **Control + Space** – opens the input source selector; press again to cycle.  
* **Command + Space** – by default opens Spotlight; you can reassign this shortcut in **System Settings → Keyboard → Keyboard Shortcuts → Spotlight** if you prefer using it for language switching.  

A small flag icon (🇮🇳) or “ह” appears in the menu bar when Hindi is active. Clicking the icon also lets you pick a different layout.

### 5. Test the layout  

Open **TextEdit**, select **Plain Text** mode, and type:  

* For INSCRIPT, press **Shift + k** → “क”.  
* For transliteration, type “namaste” → “नमस्ते”.  

If the characters appear as expected, you are ready to type Hindi on macOS.

---

## Switching Between English and Hindi Quickly  

A common workflow is to write a sentence in English, then switch to Hindi for a proper noun or phrase. The following patterns work on both platforms:

| Action | Windows | macOS |
|--------|----------|-------|
| **Toggle language** | **Windows + Space** (cycle) or **Left Alt + Shift** (within Hindi) | **Control + Space** (cycle) |
| **Show current language** | Look at the taskbar language indicator (ENG/HIN). | Look at the menu‑bar flag or “ह”. |
| **Temporary switch** (type a few characters, then revert) | Press the shortcut twice. | Press the shortcut twice. |
| **Maintain separate keyboards** (e.g., INSCRIPT for formal typing, Phonetic for casual) | Use **Left Alt + Shift** to toggle between keyboards after Hindi is selected. | Click the menu‑bar indicator and pick the desired Hindi source. |

**Practice tip:** Open a blank document and spend two minutes alternating between English and Hindi using the shortcut. Muscle memory will develop faster than memorizing the shortcut sequence.

---

## Troubleshooting Common Setup Issues  

### 1. Garbled text appears despite using a Hindi keyboard  

* **Cause:** The application is not using a Unicode‑aware font.  
* **Fix:** Ensure the document’s font supports Devanagari (e.g., **Mangal**, **Nirmala UI**, **Lohit Devanagari**, or **Arial Unicode MS**). In Windows, you can change the font in **Notepad** via **Format → Font**. On macOS, choose a Devanagari‑capable font in **TextEdit**’s format menu.

### 2. Keyboard shortcuts do not switch languages  

* **Cause:** Another app (e.g., a screen‑reader) has captured the shortcut.  
* **Fix (Windows):** Go to **Settings → Devices → Keyboard → Advanced keyboard settings → Input language hotkeys** and assign an unused combination.  
* **Fix (macOS):** Open **System Settings → Keyboard → Keyboard Shortcuts** and verify that **Control + Space** is assigned only to “Select the previous input source”.

### 3. The Hindi IME does not appear in the language bar  

* **Cause:** The language pack was not fully installed.  
* **Fix (Windows):** Return to **Language & region → Hindi → Options** and click **Download** under **Language pack**. After download, repeat the **Add a keyboard** steps.  
* **Fix (macOS):** Remove the Hindi input source from **Keyboard → Input Sources**, then add it again. If the problem persists, restart the computer.

### 4. Only half of the Devanagari characters appear (e.g., “क” shows, but “्” (halant) does not)  

* **Cause:** The font lacks the required glyph for the **Halant** (U+094D).  
* **Fix:** Switch to a font that includes the full Devanagari set, such as **Noto Sans Devanagari** (free from Google).  

### 5. Phonetic transliteration does not convert typed Roman letters  

* **Cause:** The transliteration engine is disabled or a different keyboard is active.  
* **Fix (Windows):** Verify that the **Hindi – Phonetic** keyboard is selected in the taskbar language list. If you installed a third‑party IME, ensure its background service is running (check **Task Manager** for “GoogleInputTool”).  
* **Fix (macOS):** Ensure the **Hindi – Transliteration** source is active; otherwise, the system will treat the keystrokes as plain Latin letters.

### 6. Switching works, but the cursor jumps to the wrong side of the screen  

* **Cause:** The document direction is set to **Left‑to‑Right** (LTR) while Hindi is a **Left‑to‑Right** script, but some applications enforce a **Right‑to‑Left** (RTL) layout for non‑Latin scripts.  
* **Fix:** In the application’s paragraph settings, set the text direction to **Left‑to‑Right**. In Microsoft Word, this is under **Home → Paragraph → Left‑to‑Right Text Direction**.

---

## Keeping Your Hindi Input Ready  

* **Regular updates:** Both Windows and macOS periodically release language‑support updates. Keeping the OS up‑to‑date prevents missing glyphs or IME bugs.  
* **Backup your settings:** On Windows, export your language preferences via **Settings → Time & language → Language & region → Export**. On macOS, the **Input Sources** list is stored in your user preferences and will travel with your iCloud backup.  
* **Test after changes:** Whenever you install a new application or change display scaling, open a quick test document to confirm Devanagari renders correctly.

---

## Key Takeaways  

* Activating Hindi language support installs the necessary Unicode fonts and IME components that translate keystrokes into Devanagari characters.  
* **Inscript** offers a direct key‑to‑character mapping; **Phonetic** (transliteration) lets you type Hindi by sounding out words with the Roman alphabet.  
* On **Windows**, add Hindi via **Settings → Time & language**, then install the desired keyboard under **Language options**. Use **Windows + Space** or **Left Alt + Shift** to toggle.  
* On **macOS**, add Hindi through **System Settings → Keyboard → Input Sources** and switch with **Control + Space**.  
* Common problems—garbled text, missing shortcuts, incomplete character rendering—are usually solved by selecting a proper Unicode‑capable font, confirming the correct IME is active, and ensuring OS updates are applied.  
* Quick language toggling becomes effortless with practice; the more you alternate between English and Hindi in real‑world tasks (emails, notes, social media), the more fluid your workflow will become.

modules.title: Module 3: Mastering the Inscript Keyboard Layout
modules.content:
## Why the Inscript Layout Is the Fast‑Track to Hindi Typing  

Imagine you are drafting a quick email to a colleague in Delhi. The moment you switch to Hindi, the screen fills with garbled symbols because the wrong input method is active. You pause, change the keyboard layout, and the message appears correctly: **“नमस्ते, मीटिंग कल है।”**  

That single switch—activating the standard **Inscript** layout—turns a frustrating experience into a seamless one. Inscript is the official Indian government keyboard for Devanagari; it places every Hindi letter, vowel sign (matra), and common sign on the familiar QWERTY keys, letting you type without looking away from the keyboard. Mastering this layout is the foundation for everything that follows in the later modules.

---

## The Inscript Layout at a Glance  

The layout is organized into three logical layers:

| Layer | How to access | What it contains |
|-------|----------------|-------------------|
| **Base** | Press the key alone | Primary Hindi letters (अ‑ह) and basic punctuation |
| **Shift** | Hold **Shift** while pressing the key | Secondary letters, alternate vowel signs, and the “ऋ‑ॠ” series |
| **AltGr** (or **Ctrl + Alt**) | Hold **AltGr** (or **Ctrl + Alt**) while pressing the key | Additional signs such as **ऽ**, **।**, **॥**, and the “ऍ‑ऑ” vowels |

> **Tip:** On many laptops the **AltGr** key is the right‑hand **Alt**. If your keyboard lacks a dedicated AltGr, the **Ctrl + Alt** combo works identically.

Below is the complete mapping of the 101‑key US‑English QWERTY to the standard Inscript layout. The table lists the **Base**, **Shift**, and **AltGr** characters for each physical key. (Only the alphanumeric rows are shown; the function keys are unchanged.)

| QWERTY Key | Base (Hindi) | Shift (Hindi) | AltGr (Hindi) |
|------------|--------------|---------------|---------------|
| `\``       | `ऋ` | `ॠ` | `़` |
| `1`        | `१` | `!` | `|` |
| `2`        | `२` | `@` | `@` |
| `3`        | `३` | `#` | `#` |
| `4`        | `४` | `$` | `$` |
| `5`        | `५` | `%` | `%` |
| `6`        | `६` | `^` | `^` |
| `7`        | `७` | `&` | `&` |
| `8`        | `८` | `*` | `*` |
| `9`        | `९` | `(` | `(` |
| `0`        | `०` | `)` | `)` |
| `-`        | `-` | `_` | `—` |
| `=`        | `=` | `+` | `+` |
| **Q**      | `ऋ` | `ॠ` | `़` |
| **W**      | `व` | `श` | `व॑` |
| **E**      | `ए` | `ऐ` | `ॲ` |
| **R**      | `र` | `ऱ` | `र्` |
| **T**      | `त` | `थ` | `ट` |
| **Y**      | `य` | `ऽ` | `।` |
| **U**      | `उ` | `ऊ` | `ॊ` |
| **I**      | `इ` | `ई` | `ऍ` |
| **O**      | `ओ` | `औ` | `ऑ` |
| **P**      | `प` | `फ` | `ॱ` |
| **[**      | `[` | `{` | `‘` |
| **]**      | `]` | `}` | `’` |
| **A**      | `अ` | `आ` | `अँ` |
| **S**      | `स` | `श` | `ष` |
| **D**      | `द` | `ध` | `ड` |
| **F**      | `फ` | `फ़` | `फ़` |
| **G**      | `ग` | `घ` | `ङ` |
| **H**      | `ह` | `ह़` | `ह्` |
| **J**      | `ज` | `झ` | `ज्ञ` |
| **K**      | `क` | `ख` | `क़` |
| **L**      | `ल` | `ळ` | `ऴ` |
| **;**      | `;` | `:` | `:` |
| **'**      | `'` | `"` | `"` |
| **Z**      | `ज़` | `झ़` | `ज़` |
| **X**      | `क्ष` | `क्ष़` | `क्ष्` |
| **C**      | `च` | `छ` | `छ़` |
| **V**      | `व` | `व़` | `व्` |
| **B**      | `ब` | `भ` | `ब़` |
| **N**      | `न` | `ण` | `ऩ` |
| **M**      | `म` | `ँ` | `़` |
| `,`        | `,` | `<` | `‹` |
| `.`        | `.` | `>` | `›` |
| `/`        | `/` | `?` | `़` |

> **Note:** The exact characters on the AltGr layer can vary slightly between operating‑system implementations. The table above follows the Indian Government’s “Inscript 2000” standard, which is the version used in Windows, macOS, and most Linux distributions.

---

## Understanding Primary, Shift, and AltGr Layers  

1. **Base layer** – The character you see when you press a key without any modifier. This is where you will type the majority of Hindi letters and the basic matras (vowel signs).  
2. **Shift layer** – Holding **Shift** accesses the secondary set. It contains the long‑vowel forms (आ, ई, ऊ, ए, ऐ, ओ, औ) and a few less‑frequent consonants.  
3. **AltGr layer** – This layer provides the punctuation marks and special signs that are essential for proper Devanagari orthography, such as **।** (Danda) and **ऽ** (Avagraha). It also houses the “ऍ‑ऑ” vowel letters used in transliteration of foreign words.

When you type a vowel sign (matra) you actually press the key that produces the matra **after** the consonant. For example, to write **का** you type **k** (produces क) then **a** (produces the आ‑matra ा). The Inscript layout already follows this logical order, so you never need to remember a separate “matra‑first” rule.

---

## Mapping the QWERTY Keys to Hindi Letters  

### Row‑by‑Row Walkthrough  

Below is a quick visual reference that groups the keys by their physical rows on a standard QWERTY keyboard. Use it as a cheat‑sheet while you practice.

#### Top Row (numbers and symbols)

| Key | Base | Shift |
|-----|------|-------|
| 1   | १ | ! |
| 2   | २ | @ |
| 3   | ३ | # |
| 4   | ४ | $ |
| 5   | ५ | % |
| 6   | ६ | ^ |
| 7   | ७ | & |
| 8   | ८ | * |
| 9   | ९ | ( |
| 0   | ० | ) |
| -   | - | _ |
| =   | = | + |

#### Home Row (A‑S‑D‑F‑G‑H‑J‑K‑L)

| Key | Base | Shift | AltGr |
|-----|------|-------|-------|
| A   | अ | आ | अँ |
| S   | स | श | ष |
| D   | द | ध | ड |
| F   | फ | फ़ | फ़ |
| G   | ग | घ | ङ |
| H   | ह | ह़ | ह् |
| J   | ज | झ | ज्ञ |
| K   | क | ख | क़ |
| L   | ल | ळ | ऴ |

#### Upper Row (Q‑W‑E‑R‑T‑Y‑U‑I‑O‑P)

| Key | Base | Shift | AltGr |
|-----|------|-------|-------|
| Q   | ऋ | ॠ | ़ |
| W   | व | श | व॑ |
| E   | ए | ऐ | ॲ |
| R   | र | ऱ | र् |
| T   | त | थ | ट |
| Y   | य |ऽ|।|
| U   | उ | ऊ | ॊ |
| I   | इ | ई | ऍ |
| O   | ओ | औ | ऑ |
| P   | प | फ | ॱ |

#### Bottom Row (Z‑X‑C‑V‑B‑N‑M)

| Key | Base | Shift | AltGr |
|-----|------|-------|-------|
| Z   | ज़ | झ़ | ज़ |
| X   | क्ष | क्ष़ | क्ष् |
| C   | च | छ | छ़ |
| V   | व | व़ | व् |
| B   | ब | भ | ब़ |
| N   | न | ण | ऩ |
| M   | म |ँ|़|

#### Punctuation Row

| Key | Base | Shift | AltGr |
|-----|------|-------|-------|
| ,   | , | < | ‹ |
| .   | . | > | › |
| /   | / | ? | ़ |

> **Quick‑Reference Tip:** Keep a printed or digital copy of the above tables next to your workstation for the first few days. Muscle memory will replace the need for the chart within a week.

---

## Typing Your First Hindi Words  

### Step‑by‑Step Example 1: “भारत”

1. **ब** – Press **B** (Base = ब).  
2. **ा** – Press **Shift + A** (produces the आ‑matra ा).  
3. **र** – Press **R** (Base = र).  
4. **त** – Press **T** (Base = त).  

Result: **भारत**  

> Notice how the vowel matra is typed **after** the consonant, matching the abugida principle introduced earlier.

### Step‑by‑Step Example 2: “मैं हिंदी सीख रहा हूँ”

| Character | Keys to press | Explanation |
|-----------|---------------|-------------|
| म | **M** | Base = म |
| े | **Shift + E** | ए‑matra े |
|ँ | **AltGr + M** | Chandrabindu ँ |
|   (space) | **Spacebar** | Word separator |
| ह | **H** | Base = ह |
| ि | **I** (no Shift) | इ‑matra ि placed before ह |
| न | **N** | Base = न |
| ड़ | **Shift + D** | ध‑matra ् + ड = ढ (rare; often typed as ड + ्) |
|   … | … | Continue similarly |

The full sentence appears as: **मैं हिंदी सीख रहा हूँ**  

> **Practice tip:** Type the sentence slowly, focusing on the order of consonant + matra. Once you’re comfortable, increase your speed gradually.

### Step‑by‑Step Example 3: Using AltGr – “।”

1. Hold **AltGr** (or **Ctrl + Alt**) and press **Y**.  
2. Release both keys.  

Result: **।** (Devanagari Danda, used as a full stop).  

---

## Row‑by‑Row Muscle‑Memory Drills  

The fastest way to internalize the layout is to repeat each physical row until the finger movements become automatic. Below are three progressive drills.

### Drill 1 – Single‑Row Echo

1. **Choose a row** (e.g., the Home row).  
2. **Type the base characters** in order: `अ स द फ ग ह ज क ल`.  
3. **Repeat** the same row with the Shift layer: `आ श ध फ़ घ ह़ झ ख ळ`.  
4. **Finish with AltGr**: `अँ ष ड फ़ ङ ह् ज्ञ क़ ऴ`.  

Do this for the Top, Upper, and Bottom rows. Aim for **30 seconds** per row, three repetitions.

### Drill 2 – Word‑Chain Within a Row  

Create a short phrase that uses only letters from a single row.

- **Home‑row phrase:** “**असद**” (pronounced *asada* – a nonsense word, perfect for practice).  
- **Upper‑row phrase:** “**वुरी**” (vuri).  
- **Bottom‑row phrase:** “**छबन**” (chaban).  

Type each phrase, then add the appropriate matras to turn them into real words (e.g., “असद” → “असद्” by adding Halant). This exercise forces you to locate the needed keys without looking.

### Drill 3 – Full‑Sentence Sprint  

Once you can type each row fluently, combine them into a simple sentence:

> **“भारत एक सुंदर देश है।”**  

Break the sentence into row groups:

| Segment | Keys (Base + Shift) |
|---------|--------------------|
| भारत | **B** **Shift+A** **R** **T** |
| एक | **E** **Shift+K** |
| सुंदर | **S** **U** **N** **D** **R** |
| देश | **D** **Shift+E** **Shift+S** |
| है | **H** **Shift+A** |

Practice typing the sentence three times without looking at the keyboard. After a few repetitions, you’ll notice the keys becoming second nature.

---

## Common Pitfalls and Quick Fixes  

| Problem | Why it Happens | Quick Fix |
|---------|----------------|-----------|
| **Matra appears before the consonant** | Accidentally pressing the vowel key first. | Remember the rule: **consonant → matra**. Use a finger‑placement cue (e.g., always start with the left hand for consonants). |
| **Wrong character after using Shift** | Confusing the Shift layer with the Base layer. | Keep a mental image of the two rows: the top row of letters (Base) stays the same; Shift simply adds the long‑vowel forms. |
| **AltGr characters not appearing** | Keyboard driver not recognizing AltGr, or using the wrong key combo. | Verify that the Inscript layout is active in your OS’s language settings. If AltGr still fails, use **Ctrl + Alt** instead. |
| **“ग़” vs “ग”** | Not using the AltGr‑layer for the “़” (nukta) sign. | After typing a base consonant, press **AltGr + `** (the key that produces “़”) to add the nukta. |
| **Garbage characters after copying** | Copying from a source that uses a non‑Unicode font. | Always type directly in a Unicode‑aware editor (e.g., Notepad++, VS Code, or Google Docs). |

---

## Building Speed and Accuracy – The Way Forward  

The exercises in this chapter lay the groundwork for the speed‑building techniques covered later. As you become comfortable with the row‑drills, start timing yourself with a simple stopwatch. Record:

1. **Time per row** (seconds).  
2. **Error count** (mistyped characters).  

Aim for a **10 % reduction** in time each week while keeping errors below three per minute. When you consistently achieve this, you’re ready to move on to the phonetic layouts in Module 4.

---

## Key Takeaways  

- The Inscript layout maps every Hindi letter, matra, and special sign to a specific QWERTY key, accessed via **Base**, **Shift**, or **AltGr** layers.  
- Memorizing the row‑wise tables and practicing the three drills (single‑row echo, word‑chain, full‑sentence sprint) builds the muscle memory essential for fluent typing.  
- Use **Shift** for long vowels and less‑frequent consonants; use **AltGr** (or **Ctrl + Alt**) for punctuation, the Danda, and the nukta sign.  
- Typing follows the **consonant → matra** order; this aligns with the abugida structure introduced earlier.  
- Quick‑fix strategies for common errors (matra order, Shift confusion, AltGr activation) keep you from getting stuck.  

With these foundations, you can now type Hindi confidently using the standard Inscript layout—setting the stage for higher speed, accuracy, and the more flexible phonetic keyboards that follow.

modules.title: Module 4: Using Phonetic (Transliteration) Keyboard Layouts
modules.content:
## What Is a Phonetic (Transliteration) Keyboard?

Imagine you are chatting with a friend on WhatsApp and you need to type the Hindi phrase **“क्या तुम ठीक हो?”**. You reach for the keyboard, type the English letters **“kya tum theek ho?”**, and—without touching a single Devanagari key—the screen instantly transforms into the correct Hindi script. That is the power of a **phonetic (transliteration) keyboard**: it lets you write Hindi by typing the closest English phonetics, and the input method automatically maps those phonetics to the appropriate Devanagari letters.

Unlike the Inscript layout, which requires you to memorize the exact position of each Devanagari character, the phonetic layout leverages the **sound‑to‑letter correspondence** you already know from speaking Hindi. This makes it especially attractive for beginners who can start typing meaningful sentences right away.

---

## Getting Started with the Phonetic Layout

### Activating the Phonetic Input Method
1. **Open the language settings** you configured in *Module 2*.  
2. **Select the phonetic option** (often labeled “Hindi – Phonetic” or “Hindi – Transliteration”).  
3. **Confirm the activation**; you should now see a language indicator (e.g., “हिंदी (फ़ोनेटिक)”) on your taskbar or menu bar.

> **Tip:** Most operating systems let you toggle between installed keyboards with `Alt + Shift` (Windows), `Command + Space` (macOS) or `Super + Space` (Linux). Keep this shortcut handy; you’ll use it constantly while you practice switching between phonetic and native layouts.

### Switching on the Fly
When you need to insert an English word or a technical term inside a Hindi sentence, simply press the shortcut again to switch to your standard English layout, type the word, then switch back. The input method remembers the last phonetic string you typed, so you can resume Hindi typing without any loss of context.

---

## Core Mapping Rules

Phonetic keyboards follow a **consistent set of rules** that translate the Latin letters you type into Devanagari characters. Understanding these rules lets you predict the output even before you see it on the screen.

| **Latin Input** | **Devanagari Output** | **Explanation** |
|----------------|----------------------|-----------------|
| a, aa, i, ii, u, uu, e, ai, o, au | अ, आ, इ, ई, उ, ऊ, ए, ऐ, ओ, औ | Vowel letters are produced when the vowel appears **at the beginning of a word** or **after a space**. |
| k, kh, g, gh, ṅ | क, ख, ग, घ, ङ | Consonants are entered directly. |
| n, ny, m, mh | न, ञ, म, ं (anusvara) | Special consonants and the anusvara are mapped by their usual Latin equivalents. |
| . (dot) | । | Typing a period after a Hindi word produces the Devanagari danda. |
| ' (single quote) | ऽ | The avagraha (used rarely) can be entered with a single quote after a consonant. |

> **Remember:** Every consonant carries an **inherent vowel “अ”** unless you explicitly suppress it with the halant (virama). This is the same rule you learned in *Module 1* for independent letters and matras.

---

### Common Sound Mappings

Below is a quick‑reference table for the most frequently used sounds. The left column shows the **phonetic string** you type; the right column shows the **resulting Devanagari character**.

| Phonetic | Devanagari |
|----------|------------|
| ka | क |
| kha | ख |
| ga | ग |
| gha | घ |
| cha | च |
| chha | छ |
| ja | ज |
| jha | झ |
| ṭa | ट |
| ṭha | ठ |
| ḍa | ड |
| ḍha | ढ |
| na | न |
| pa | प |
| pha | फ |
| ba | ब |
| bha | भ |
| ma | म |
| ya | य |
| ra | र |
| la | ल |
| va | व |
| śa | श |
| ṣa | ष |
| sa | स |
| ha | ह |
| ṣa | ष |
| kṣa | क्ष |
| tr | त्र |
| jñ | ज्ञ |

*Tip:* The **“kṣa”** mapping automatically produces the ligature **“क्ष”** (U+0915 + U+094D + U+0937) without you needing to type the halant manually.

---

## Vowel Diacritics (Matras) in Transliteration

When a vowel follows a consonant, the phonetic layout automatically converts the vowel **into a matra**, attaching it to the preceding consonant. This mirrors the way matras were introduced in *Module 1*.

| **Typed Sequence** | **Resulting Devanagari** | **Matra Description** |
|-------------------|--------------------------|------------------------|
| k + a | क | No matra (inherent “अ”) |
| k + aa | का | Long “आ” matra (ा) |
| k + i | कि | Short “इ” matra (ि) |
| k + ii | की | Long “ई” matra (ी) |
| k + u | कु | Short “उ” matra (ु) |
| k + uu | कू | Long “ऊ” matra (ू) |
| k + e | के | “ए” matra (े) |
| k + ai | कै | “ऐ” matra (ै) |
| k + o | को | “ओ” matra (ो) |
| k + au | कौ | “औ” matra (ौ) |

**Example:**  
Type **“swaagat”** → **स्वागत**  
- `s` → स  
- `w` (for “व”) → व (the layout treats “w” as the “व” sound)  
- `a` after “व” → व + “अ” matra = वै (but because “a” is the inherent vowel, no visible matra appears)  
- `g` → ग  
- `a` after “g” → ग + “अ” → ग (inherent)  
- `t` → त  

The engine intelligently combines the pieces to produce **स्वागत**.

---

## The Halant (Virama) and Conjunct Consonants

### Inserting the Halant

To suppress the inherent “अ” and join two consonants, you need to type the **halant**. In most phonetic layouts this is achieved by:

- **Pressing the “`” (back‑tick) key** after the first consonant, **or**  
- **Appending an explicit “\”** (backslash) before the next consonant.

Both methods insert the Unicode **halant (U+094D)**.

**Example 1:** Typing “k\sh” → क् + श = क्ष  
**Example 2:** Typing “k`sh” → क् + श = क्ष (same result)

### Forming Common Conjuncts

| **Phonetic Input** | **Devanagari Output** | **Explanation** |
|--------------------|----------------------|-----------------|
| k`sh | क्ष | Halant after “k” + “sh” |
| tr | त्र | Direct mapping for the common conjunct “त्र” |
| j`ñ | ज्ञ | Halant after “j” + “ñ” |
| s`t | स्त | Halant after “s” + “t” |
| n`d | ंड | Halant after “n” + “d” (used in words like “बन्ध”) |

### Step‑by‑Step Conjunct Construction

1. **Type the first consonant** (e.g., `k`).  
2. **Insert the halant** (`\` or `` ` ``). The screen now shows **क्**.  
3. **Type the second consonant** (e.g., `sh`). The layout automatically merges the two parts into **क्ष**.  
4. **Add a vowel** if needed (e.g., `aa` after the conjunct) → **क्षा**.

---

## Typing Frequently Used Words Without Memorizing Key Positions

Because the phonetic layout relies on sound rather than position, you can type whole words directly. Below are **20 everyday Hindi words** and the exact keystrokes you need. Practice each until the output appears automatically.

| **English Phonetics** | **Devanagari** |
|-----------------------|----------------|
| namaste               | नमस्ते |
| dhanyavaad            | धन्यवाद |
| kripya                | कृपया |
| shukriya              | शुक्रिया |
| aapka                 | आपका |
| tumhara               | तुम्हारा |
| kaun                  | कौन |
| kyon                  | क्यों |
| kaise                 | कैसे |
| kya                   | क्या |
| bhavishya             | भविष्य |
| safar                 | सफ़र |
| school                | स्कूल |
| hospital              | हॉस्पिटल |
| kitab                 | किताब |
| paani                 | पानी |
| roti                  | रोटी |
| gaadi                 | गाड़ी |
| samay                 | समय |
| dosti                 | दोस्ती |

**Practice Exercise:** Open a blank document, switch to the phonetic layout, and type the list above without looking at any reference. After each word, verify that the Devanagari output matches the table. This reinforces the **sound‑to‑letter mapping** and builds muscle memory for common sequences.

---

## Switching Seamlessly Between Phonetic and Native Layouts

Real‑world typing often requires **mixing scripts**—for example, a Hindi sentence that contains an English brand name or a numeric code. Here’s a workflow that keeps you in control:

1. **Start in Phonetic Mode** – type the Hindi portion.  
2. **Trigger the shortcut** (`Alt + Shift` on Windows) to switch to the English layout.  
3. **Enter the English word or number** (e.g., “Google”, “2024”).  
4. **Switch back** to phonetic mode and continue typing Hindi.

### Maintaining Cursor Position

When you toggle layouts, the cursor stays exactly where you left it, so you can interleave scripts without breaking the sentence flow. If you notice the cursor jumping to the start of the line, check that you are using the **system‑wide** shortcut rather than a per‑application shortcut that may reset the caret.

### Using the Language Bar for Quick Access

Most OS language bars allow you to **click the script icon** (e.g., “हिं” for Hindi) to switch layouts. This visual cue is helpful when you are still learning the keyboard shortcut.

---

## Troubleshooting Common Issues

| **Problem** | **Likely Cause** | **Quick Fix** |
|-------------|------------------|---------------|
| Unexpected English letters appear (e.g., “kha” becomes “kha” instead of “खा”). | The layout is still set to **Inscript** or another native mode. | Verify the active input method; switch to “Hindi – Phonetic”. |
| Double letters (e.g., “aa” yields “आा”). | You typed the vowel **after** a consonant that already had the same matra. | Remember that a vowel after a consonant **replaces** the inherent “अ”; you don’t need to type it twice. |
| Conjunct not forming (e.g., “ksh” stays as “कश”). | Halant not inserted. | Use the back‑tick or backslash **immediately after** the first consonant before typing the second. |
| Autocorrect changes “ra” to “रa”. | The input method’s auto‑completion feature is on. | Turn off “auto‑replace” in the input method settings, or press `Ctrl + Z` to undo the change. |

If you encounter a character that looks like **garbled text**, it usually indicates a **Unicode mismatch**—the application may not support Devanagari fonts. Ensure the document’s font is set to a Unicode‑compatible Hindi font (e.g., “Mangal”, “Noto Sans Devanagari”).

---

## Practice Activity: A Real‑World Scenario

**Scenario:** You need to send a short email to a colleague in Hindi, mentioning a project deadline, a meeting time, and a reference to a shared Google Drive folder.

**Required Sentence (in Hindi):**  

> “नमस्ते राज, कृपया 15 जुलाई को शाम 5 बजे हमारी मीटिंग के लिए तैयार रहें। फ़ाइलें यहाँ हैं: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/XYZ”

**Step‑by‑Step Typing Using Phonetic Layout**

| **Keystrokes** | **Result** |
|----------------|------------|
| namaste        | नमस्ते |
| (space)        | (space) |
| raj,           | राज, |
| (space)        | (space) |
| kripya         | कृपया |
| (space)        | (space) |
| 15             | 15 |
| (space)        | (space) |
| julai          | जुलाई |
| (space)        | (space) |
| ko             | को |
| (space)        | (space) |
| shaam          | शाम |
| (space)        | (space) |
| 5              | 5 |
| (space)        | (space) |
| baje           | बजे |
| (space)        | (space) |
| hamari         | हमारी |
| (space)        | (space) |
| meeting        | मीटिंग |
| (space)        | (space) |
| ke             | के |
| (space)        | (space) |
| liye           | लिए |
| (space)        | (space) |
| taiyar         | तैयार |
| (space)        | (space) |
| rahen.         | रहें। |
| (Enter)        | (new line) |
| filein         | फ़ाइलें |
| yahan          | यहाँ |
| hain:          | हैं: |
| (space)        | (space) |
| (switch to English) | https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/XYZ |

Notice how the **English URL** is typed after a quick layout switch, then you switch back to continue the Hindi text. Practicing this exact workflow will cement the habit of **seamless switching** and reinforce the phonetic mappings you have learned.

---

## Key Takeaways

- Phonetic (transliteration) keyboards let you type Hindi by entering **English phonetics**, which the system automatically converts to Devanagari.
- The **core mapping rules** align Latin letters with Hindi sounds; vowels typed at the start of a word become independent letters, while vowels after a consonant become **matras**.
- Use the **halant** (`\` or `` ` ``) to suppress the inherent “अ” and create **conjunct consonants** (e.g., “k`sh” → “क्ष”).
- Frequent words can be typed directly without memorizing key positions; practice with the provided word list to build fluency.
- Switching between **phonetic and native layouts** is achieved via OS shortcuts (`Alt + Shift`, `Command + Space`, etc.) or the language bar, allowing you to intermix Hindi and English effortlessly.
- When unexpected characters appear, verify that the phonetic layout is active, and ensure your document uses a Unicode‑compatible Devanagari font.

modules.title: Module 5: Building Speed and Accuracy
modules.content:
## Why Speed and Accuracy Matter  

Imagine you are drafting a short email in Hindi to a colleague in Delhi. You type “धन्यवाद” and hit **Enter**—the message is sent instantly, and the recipient smiles because the text appears exactly as intended. Now picture the same email typed a few minutes later, with half‑finished words, misplaced matras, and a garbled “धनवद्” that forces the reader to pause and decode. The difference isn’t just cosmetic; it affects how professionally you are perceived and how efficiently you can communicate.  

For beginners, the first milestone is to type **comfortably fast** while keeping **errors low**. This chapter shows you how to measure, set, and achieve those milestones using simple tools and disciplined practice.

---

## Understanding Typing Metrics  

Before you can improve, you need a clear picture of where you stand today. Two numbers dominate the conversation:

| Metric | What It Means | Why It Helps |
|--------|---------------|--------------|
| **Words‑per‑minute (WPM)** | Number of standard five‑character “words” typed in one minute. | Indicates raw speed. |
| **Accuracy (%)** | Ratio of correctly typed characters to total characters entered. | Shows how clean your output is. |

A **standard word** in typing tests is five characters, regardless of the language. For Hindi, a “word” may be shorter or longer than five Devanagari characters, but the test’s algorithm normalises the count. When you first try a test, you’ll likely see a low WPM and a modest accuracy (e.g., 12 WPM, 78 %). Both figures will improve as you follow the routines below.

---

## Choosing the Right Online Typing Tester  

A reliable tester gives you consistent numbers, a clean interface, and the ability to focus on Hindi script. Here are three popular, free options (as of 2026) that meet those criteria:

1. **TypingBaba – Hindi**  
   *Pros*: Dedicated Hindi mode, supports both Inscript and phonetic layouts, displays real‑time WPM and error count.  
   *Cons*: Limited custom word list import.

2. **10FastFingers – Hindi**  
   *Pros*: Large community leaderboard, allows you to upload your own word list (useful for curated practice).  
   *Cons*: Advertisements may distract beginners.

3. **Keybr.com – Custom Language**  
   *Pros*: Generates algorithmic drills based on your error patterns, excellent for targeting weak matras or conjuncts.  
   *Cons*: Requires a small amount of configuration to switch the keyboard to Hindi.

**How to pick**:  
- **First‑time users** should start with TypingBaba for its simplicity.  
- **Goal‑oriented learners** who want to track specific characters (e.g., “क्ष”, “त्र”) may prefer Keybr.com.  
- **Competitive spirits** can try 10FastFingers to benchmark against other Hindi typists.

---

## Setting Incremental Speed Goals  

### 1. Establish a Baseline  

1. **Run a 1‑minute test** on your chosen platform.  
2. Record **WPM** and **Accuracy** in a notebook or spreadsheet.  
3. Note any recurring mistakes (e.g., confusion between “ि” and “ी”, mis‑placement of the halant).

### 2. Apply the SMART Framework  

- **Specific** – “Increase my WPM from 12 to 18 while keeping accuracy above 90 %.”  
- **Measurable** – Use the tester’s numeric read‑out.  
- **Achievable** – Raise the target by 5‑10 % each week, not by 100 % overnight.  
- **Relevant** – Align the goal with real‑world needs (e.g., typing a 200‑word essay).  
- **Time‑bound** – “Reach 18 WPM within 10 days.”

### 3. Break Goals into Mini‑Milestones  

| Week | Target WPM | Minimum Accuracy |
|------|------------|-------------------|
| 1    | 15         | 88 %              |
| 2    | 18         | 90 %              |
| 3    | 22         | 92 %              |
| 4    | 25         | 94 %              |

Write these milestones in the same sheet where you log daily scores; visual progress bars help maintain motivation.

---

## Tracking Progress Over Time  

A simple **Google Sheet** or **Excel workbook** is enough. Create columns for:

- **Date**  
- **Test Platform** (TypingBaba, etc.)  
- **WPM**  
- **Accuracy**  
- **Error Type** (e.g., “matra swap”, “halant missing”)  
- **Notes** (fatigue, distractions)

Use the built‑in chart feature to plot **WPM** and **Accuracy** side‑by‑side. A rising WPM curve that stays above the 90 % accuracy line signals healthy growth. If accuracy dips sharply when speed jumps, you’ve identified a **speed‑accuracy trade‑off** that needs corrective work.

---

## Structured Practice with Curated Hindi Word Lists  

### 1. Why Word Lists Matter  

Hindi’s abugida nature means many characters combine **consonant + matra** forms, and the presence of **conjuncts** (e.g., “क्ष”, “त्र”) can slow a typist down. Targeted word lists let you rehearse the most trouble‑prone clusters repeatedly.

### 2. Sample Word Lists  

| Category | Example Words (Inscript) | Focus |
|----------|--------------------------|-------|
| **Simple Vowels** | “अ”, “इ”, “ऊ”, “ए”, “ओ” | Independent vowel letters |
| **Matra‑Heavy** | “किताब”, “सूरज”, “मित्र”, “प्याला” | Vowel signs attached to consonants |
| **Conjunct‑Rich** | “क्षत्री”, “श्रद्धा”, “त्रिकोण”, “ज्योति” | Halant‑based ligatures |
| **Nasals & Diacritics** | “अँधेरा”, “संख्या”, “हिंदी”, “गाँव” | Anusvara, Chandrabindu, Visarga |
| **Numbers & Punctuation** | “१२३, ४५६; ७८९.” | Devanagari numerals, punctuation (for later modules) |

You can copy‑paste these lists into the custom‑word‑list feature of 10FastFingers or upload a plain‑text file to Keybr.com.

### 3. Daily Word Drills  

1. **Select a category** (e.g., Matra‑Heavy).  
2. **Type each word** slowly, focusing on correct placement of the matra.  
3. **Repeat** until you can type the full list at least **3 times** without looking at the keyboard.

Progressively rotate categories each day to ensure balanced exposure.

---

## Sentence‑Level Practice  

Words in isolation are useful, but sentences force you to manage **spacing**, **punctuation**, and **contextual flow**. Use the following short, everyday sentences (written in Inscript):

1. **“मैं दिल्ली जा रहा हूँ।”** – Simple present tense.  
2. **“क्या आप हिन्दी समझते हैं?”** – Question form with “क्या”.  
3. **“कल हमने नई पुस्तक खरीदी।”** – Past tense with “नयी”.  
4. **“वह जल्दी नहीं आती।”** – Negative construction.  

**Practice Routine**  

- **Read** the sentence aloud once.  
- **Type** it without looking at the screen; after each attempt, compare to the original.  
- **Mark** any misplaced matras (e.g., “ि” appearing before the consonant) and correct them immediately.  

Over weeks, expand the pool to longer paragraphs—news headlines, short stories, or social‑media posts—so you develop stamina.

---

## Error‑Reduction Techniques  

### Finger Placement Revisited  

Even though the Inscript layout was covered earlier, a **micro‑adjustment** can shave seconds off each keystroke:

- **Home Row Anchor**: Keep the index fingers on “द” (right hand) and “ज” (left hand).  
- **Thumbs**: Rest on the space bar; use a light tap rather than a heavy press to avoid fatigue.  
- **Rolling Motion**: For common consonant‑matra pairs like “कि” (क + ि), let the left index finger strike “क” while the right index slides to “ि”. This keeps both hands active and reduces the need to shift the left hand away from the home row.

### Visual Focus Strategies  

- **Peripheral Vision**: Train yourself to glance at the **next word** while still typing the current one. This mirrors the way professional typists maintain a flow.  
- **Screen‑Only Glance**: After the first week, aim to keep your eyes on the monitor 90 % of the time. Use a **transparent overlay** (e.g., a faint grid) if you find yourself drifting back to the keyboard.

### Rhythm and Timing  

- **Metronome Method**: Set a metronome to 60 BPM (beats per minute). Each beat corresponds to a keystroke. Start slow, then gradually increase the tempo as accuracy remains high.  
- **Chunking**: Group characters into logical units—**consonant + matra**, **conjunct**, **punctuation**—and type each chunk as a single rhythmic pulse.

---

## Building a Daily Practice Routine  

| Phase | Duration | Activity |
|-------|----------|----------|
| **Warm‑up** | 2 min | Light finger stretches, 30‑second “home‑row” tap drill. |
| **Metric Check** | 1 min | Run a 30‑second mini‑test on your chosen platform; record numbers. |
| **Word Drills** | 8 min | Rotate through the five curated categories (≈1 min per category). |
| **Sentence Practice** | 5 min | Type two sentences from the list; focus on fluidity. |
| **Error Review** | 3 min | Look at the mistakes flagged by the tester; repeat the problematic words. |
| **Cool‑down** | 1 min | Gentle hand shake, deep breathing, log the day’s results. |

Total: **20 minutes**. Consistency beats marathon sessions; a 20‑minute daily habit yields more sustainable gains than a 2‑hour weekend binge.

---

## Dealing with Plateaus and Frustration  

- **Micro‑Goal Reset**: If you stall (e.g., WPM stays at 18 for three days), lower the weekly target by 2 WPM and add an extra 5‑minute focus drill on the most error‑prone matras.  
- **Swap Layouts Temporarily**: Switching from Inscript to a phonetic layout for a short session can refresh muscle memory and reveal hidden weaknesses. Return to Inscript afterward with a clearer perspective.  
- **Physical Breaks**: The brain’s ability to encode motor patterns drops after 30 minutes of continuous typing. A 5‑minute walk or stretch can revive concentration.

---

## Quick Checklist for a Practice Session  

- [ ] Keyboard is set to the correct Hindi layout (Inscript).  
- [ ] Hands are positioned on the home row; thumbs resting on space.  
- [ ] Metronome (if used) is set to the desired tempo.  
- [ ] Word list for the day is loaded into the tester.  
- [ ] Accuracy target (≥ 90 %) is visible on screen.  
- [ ] Errors from the previous session are reviewed before starting.  
- [ ] End‑of‑session log is updated with WPM, accuracy, and notes.  

Keep this checklist printed and tape it beside your workstation—visual reminders reinforce disciplined practice.

---

## Key Takeaways  

- **Measure first**: Use an online Hindi typing tester to obtain baseline **WPM** and **accuracy** numbers.  
- **Set SMART goals**: Incremental targets (5‑10 % weekly) keep progress realistic and motivating.  
- **Track systematically**: A simple spreadsheet visualises trends and highlights error patterns.  
- **Practice with purpose**: Curated word lists (vowel‑heavy, conjunct‑rich, nasal‑diacritics) and short sentences build fluency in the most challenging script elements.  
- **Apply error‑reduction tactics**: Precise finger placement, peripheral visual focus, and rhythmic chunking dramatically cut mistakes.  
- **Maintain a consistent routine**: A 20‑minute daily cycle—warm‑up, metric check, drills, review—outperforms irregular, longer sessions.  
- **Adapt when stuck**: Lower targets, switch layouts briefly, or take physical breaks to overcome plateaus.  

By integrating measurement, goal‑setting, targeted drills, and ergonomic techniques, you will steadily transform from a cautious beginner into a confident Hindi typist capable of producing clean, rapid text—ready for the more advanced shortcuts and real‑world applications awaiting in the later modules.

modules.title: Module 6: Essential Hindi Keyboard Shortcuts
modules.content:
## Speed Meets Simplicity: A Real‑World Typing Sprint  

Imagine you are drafting a short announcement for a community event in Hindi:  

> “सभी को आमंत्रण – अगले शनिवार को हमारे गाँव में पुस्तक मेले का आयोजन होगा।”  

You have already typed the sentence, but now you need to **copy it**, **paste it** into a flyer, **bold the title**, and **undo** a stray extra space. You could reach for the mouse each time, but a seasoned typist knows that a handful of keystrokes can finish the job in seconds. This chapter shows exactly how those keystrokes work—both the universal shortcuts you already use in English and the Hindi‑specific tweaks that keep Devanagari text flowing smoothly.

---

## 1. The Universal Shortcuts Every Hindi Typist Needs  

Even when you are working with Hindi, the operating system and most word processors treat the text as a series of Unicode code points. The **clipboard** (the temporary storage area for copied or cut text) works the same way, so the classic shortcuts are fully functional.

| Shortcut | Action | Hindi‑specific tip |
|----------|--------|--------------------|
| **Ctrl + C** | Copy the selected text to the clipboard | Works on Devanagari letters, matras, and ligatures exactly as on Latin script. |
| **Ctrl + V** | Paste the clipboard contents at the cursor | If you paste into a line that already contains a halant (्), the new characters will automatically join the existing conjunct. |
| **Ctrl + X** | Cut (remove) the selected text and copy it | Useful for moving whole words or phrases—e.g., cutting “पुस्तक मेले” to reposition it. |
| **Ctrl + Z** | Undo the last action | Undo is especially handy after an accidental **halant** that creates an unwanted ligature. |
| **Ctrl + Y** (or **Ctrl + Shift + Z**) | Redo the undone action | Restores the text you just undid, preserving the original Unicode sequence. |
| **Ctrl + A** | Select **all** text in the current document | A quick way to apply a style change to the entire Hindi document. |
| **Ctrl + S** | Save the current file | Remember to save often, particularly when working with complex Devanagari scripts that may not render correctly until saved. |
| **Ctrl + F** | Open the Find dialog | Search works on Unicode code points, so you can look for a specific vowel sign (e.g., “ा”) or a particular conjunct. |

> **Practice tip:** Open a blank document, type a short Hindi paragraph, then use **Ctrl + A** followed by **Ctrl + C** and **Ctrl + V** into a new document. Notice that the copied text retains all matras and ligatures exactly as you typed them.

---

## 2. Navigating Hindi Documents Efficiently  

When typing in Hindi, you often need to move the cursor across characters that consist of a base consonant plus one or more matras. The arrow keys, Home/End, and Page navigation shortcuts treat each **grapheme cluster** (the visual unit you see on screen) as a single step, which makes navigation intuitive once you get used to it.

### 2.1 Arrow Keys and Their Hindi Behaviour  

| Key | Moves the cursor … | Example on “कुमार” |
|-----|-------------------|---------------------|
| **← (Left Arrow)** | One grapheme cluster to the left (e.g., from “र” to “ा”) | From “र” → “ा” |
| **→ (Right Arrow)** | One grapheme cluster to the right (e.g., from “ु” to “र”) | From “ु” → “र” |
| **↑ (Up Arrow)** | Same column on the line above | Useful in tables or multi‑line drafts. |
| **↓ (Down Arrow)** | Same column on the line below | Same as above. |

> **Why it matters:** A Devanagari vowel sign (matra) appears **to the left** of its consonant (e.g., “ि” in “कि”). The left arrow still moves you **backward** to the preceding grapheme, not into the middle of the matra. This prevents you from accidentally splitting a cluster.

### 2.2 Home, End, and Their Hindi Variants  

* **Home** – jumps to the beginning of the current line. In Hindi, it lands **before the first visible grapheme**, which may be a leading matra or a punctuation mark.  
* **End** – jumps to the line’s end, positioning the cursor **after the last grapheme** (including any trailing halant).  

These shortcuts are invaluable when you need to add a heading or a concluding phrase without scrolling.

### 2.3 Page Navigation  

| Shortcut | Action |
|----------|--------|
| **Page Up** | Scrolls the view up one screenful while keeping the cursor position. |
| **Page Down** | Scrolls down one screenful. |
| **Ctrl + Page Up** | Moves to the previous tab (in browsers or multi‑document editors). |
| **Ctrl + Page Down** | Moves to the next tab. |

When reviewing a lengthy Hindi report, combine **Page Down** with **Ctrl + F** to quickly locate a specific term.

### 2.4 Jumping Word‑by‑Word in Hindi  

Most editors support **Ctrl + ←/→** to move the cursor a whole word at a time. In Devanagari, a “word” is defined by spaces and punctuation, so the shortcut skips over entire phrases like “समाचार” or “दिल्ली”. This works even when a word contains multiple conjuncts.

> **Exercise:** Type the sentence “आज दिल्ली में बहुत तेज़ हवा चल रही है।” Use **Ctrl + ←** and **Ctrl + →** repeatedly. Count how many keystrokes it takes to move from the start of the line to the end.

---

## 3. Switching Between Hindi and English Input  

A bilingual document often requires frequent toggling between Hindi and English. Modern operating systems provide two reliable methods: **Alt + Shift** and **Win + Space** (Windows) or **Option + Command + Space** (macOS). Both shortcuts cycle through the installed input languages.

### 3.1 Configuring the Shortcut  

1. **Windows 10/11:**  
   *Open Settings → Time & Language → Language & Region → Keyboard.*  
   *Ensure “Hindi (India)” and “English (United States)” are listed.*  
   *The default toggle is **Alt + Shift**; you can also enable **Win + Space** under Advanced keyboard settings.*

2. **macOS:**  
   *Open System Settings → Keyboard → Input Sources.*  
   *Add “Hindi – Inscript” and “U.S.” if they are not present.*  
   *Enable “Show Input menu in menu bar” and set the shortcut to **Control + Space** (or **Option + Command + Space**).*

### 3.2 Using the Shortcut in Practice  

| Situation | Desired Action | Shortcut |
|-----------|----------------|----------|
| You are typing a Hindi paragraph and need to insert an English URL (“www.example.com”) | Switch to English input, type the URL, then switch back | **Alt + Shift** (or **Win + Space**) → type → **Alt + Shift** again |
| You want to quickly insert a Hindi proper noun inside an English sentence | Same as above | Same shortcut |

**Tip:** After toggling, the **language indicator** (often a two‑letter code like “EN” or “HI”) appears on the taskbar or menu bar. Keep an eye on it; a missed toggle is a common source of garbled text.

### 3.3 Avoiding “Garbled Text” When Switching  

If you type a few characters in the wrong language, the Unicode code points may not render as expected, producing boxes or unrelated symbols. The quickest remedy is:

1. **Undo** the mistaken characters (**Ctrl + Z**).  
2. **Switch** to the correct language.  
3. **Retype** the segment.

Because the undo stack stores the raw Unicode, you won’t lose surrounding Hindi characters.

---

## 4. Formatting Hindi Text with Keyboard Shortcuts  

Beyond plain typing, you will often need to format headings, emphasize words, or adjust paragraph alignment. Most word processors (Microsoft Word, Google Docs, LibreOffice Writer) share a common set of formatting shortcuts. The key is to remember that **bold**, **italic**, and **underline** apply to the selected Unicode characters, regardless of script.

| Shortcut | Formatting Action | Hindi Example |
|----------|-------------------|---------------|
| **Ctrl + B** | Toggle **Bold** | “**समाचार**” becomes “**समाचार**”. |
| **Ctrl + I** | Toggle *Italic* | “*पुस्तक*” becomes “*पुस्तक*”. |
| **Ctrl + U** | Toggle _Underline_ | “_घटना_” becomes “_घटना_”. |
| **Ctrl + L** | Align Left | Useful for left‑aligned Hindi text in bilingual columns. |
| **Ctrl + R** | Align Right | Aligns Hindi text to the right edge—common in formal letters. |
| **Ctrl + E** | Center Align | Centers a Hindi title such as “**वार्षिक सम्मेलन**”. |
| **Ctrl + T** | Increase **Indent** | Indents a Hindi bullet point. |
| **Ctrl + Shift + T** | Decrease **Indent** | Removes an extra indent. |
| **Ctrl + Shift + >** | Increase Font Size | Makes a Hindi heading larger. |
| **Ctrl + Shift + <** | Decrease Font Size | Shrinks body text. |

### 4.1 Applying Formatting to a Selection  

1. **Select** the Hindi text with the mouse or **Shift + ←/→**.  
2. Press the desired shortcut (e.g., **Ctrl + B**).  
3. The formatting instantly appears; the underlying Unicode remains unchanged.

> **Note:** If you are using a **phonetic** input method (Module 4), the formatting shortcuts work the same way. The input method only affects how characters are entered, not how they are styled.

### 4.2 Using Styles for Consistent Hindi Documents  

Most word processors let you define **styles** (e.g., “Heading 1”, “Normal”, “Quote”). Assigning a style to Hindi text ensures uniform fonts, sizes, and spacing. Keyboard shortcuts to apply styles are:

* **Alt + Ctrl + 1** – Apply “Heading 1”.  
* **Alt + Ctrl + 2** – Apply “Heading 2”.  
* **Alt + Ctrl + 0** – Apply “Normal”.

When you press **Alt + Ctrl + 1**, the selected Hindi heading instantly adopts the predefined “Heading 1” attributes (often a larger, bold Devanagari font). This is far faster than manually clicking the style dropdown.

---

## 5. Putting It All Together – A Mini‑Exercise  

Below is a step‑by‑step task that incorporates every shortcut covered so far. Work on a fresh document in your preferred word processor.

1. **Create a title**  
   * Type “**समुदायिक पुस्तक मेले की घोषणा**”.  
   * Select the line and press **Ctrl + B** and **Ctrl + Shift + >** to make it bold and larger.  

2. **Insert an English URL**  
   * Press **Alt + Shift** to switch to English.  
   * Type “www.booksfair.in”.  
   * Switch back to Hindi with **Alt + Shift**.  

3. **Write a body paragraph**  
   * Type: “हम सभी को इस शनिवार को पुस्तक मेले में भाग लेने के लिए आमंत्रित करते हैं।”  

4. **Bold a key phrase**  
   * Highlight “पुस्तक मेले”.  
   * Press **Ctrl + B**.  

5. **Correct a mistake**  
   * Accidentally typed “पुस्तक् मेले”.  
   * Press **Ctrl + Z** to undo, then delete the stray halant (्) and retype “पुस्तक”.  

6. **Navigate to the end of the paragraph**  
   * Press **End** to jump to the line’s end.  

7. **Add a concluding line**  
   * Press **Enter**, then type “धन्यवाद!”  

8. **Center the title**  
   * Click anywhere on the title line.  
   * Press **Ctrl + E**.  

9. **Save the document**  
   * Press **Ctrl + S** and give it a name like “BookFair_Announcement.docx”.  

You have now used **copy/paste**, **language toggling**, **navigation**, **formatting**, **undo**, and **saving**—all with keyboard shortcuts alone. Repeating this exercise a few times will cement the muscle memory needed for real‑world typing speed.

---

## 6. Troubleshooting Common Shortcut Issues  

| Symptom | Likely Cause | Quick Fix |
|----------|--------------|-----------|
| **Ctrl + C/V/X does nothing** | The document is in **read‑only** mode or the selection is empty. | Ensure the document is editable and actually select text (use **Shift + ←/→**). |
| **Alt + Shift toggles language but the indicator doesn’t change** | Multiple input languages are installed; Windows cycles through all of them. | Open **Settings → Time & Language → Keyboard** and remove any unwanted languages. |
| **Bold/Italic shortcuts affect only part of a Hindi conjunct** | The selection landed in the middle of a grapheme cluster. | Use **Shift + ←/→** to select whole clusters, or double‑click the word to select it entirely. |
| **Page Up/Down scrolls but the cursor jumps to an unexpected place** | The cursor was at the document’s start/end before scrolling. | Move the cursor to the middle of the page before using Page navigation, or use **Ctrl + Home/End** to reposition. |
| **Undo (Ctrl + Z) reverts more than intended** | The application groups multiple edits into a single undo step (common in Google Docs). | Use **Ctrl + Shift + Z** (Redo) to step forward, or adjust the editor’s undo settings if available. |

---

## 7. Adapting Shortcuts to Different Operating Systems  

While the table above focuses on Windows, macOS and many Linux desktop environments provide analogous shortcuts:

| Action | Windows Shortcut | macOS Shortcut |
|--------|------------------|----------------|
| Copy | **Ctrl + C** | **Command + C** |
| Paste | **Ctrl + V** | **Command + V** |
| Cut | **Ctrl + X** | **Command + X** |
| Undo | **Ctrl + Z** | **Command + Z** |
| Redo | **Ctrl + Y** or **Ctrl + Shift + Z** | **Command + Shift + Z** |
| Switch Language | **Alt + Shift** / **Win + Space** | **Control + Space** (or **Option + Command + Space**) |
| Bold | **Ctrl + B** | **Command + B** |
| Italic | **Ctrl + I** | **Command + I** |
| Underline | **Ctrl + U** | **Command + U** |
| Align Left | **Ctrl + L** | **Command + Option + L** |
| Align Right | **Ctrl + R** | **Command + Option + R** |
| Center | **Ctrl + E** | **Command + Option + C** |

The underlying logic remains the same; only the modifier key changes from **Ctrl** to **Command**. If you work across platforms, practice the macOS equivalents to maintain speed.

---

## 8. Building a Personal Shortcut Cheat Sheet  

A quick reference sheet can reinforce learning. Here’s a concise layout you can copy into a sticky note or a digital note app:

```
Copy / Cut / Paste      : Ctrl+C / Ctrl+X / Ctrl+V
Undo / Redo            : Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y
Select All / Save      : Ctrl+A / Ctrl+S
Bold / Italic / Underline : Ctrl+B / Ctrl+I / Ctrl+U
Align L / R / C        : Ctrl+L / Ctrl+R / Ctrl+E
Increase / Decrease Size: Ctrl+Shift+> / Ctrl+Shift+<
Switch Language         : Alt+Shift (Win+Space)
Navigate: ← → ↑ ↓      : Arrow keys
Home / End             : Home / End
Page Up / Down         : PageUp / PageDown
```

Print it, keep it near your keyboard, and glance at it whenever you feel stuck. Over time the shortcuts will become second nature.

---

## Key Takeaways  

- **Universal shortcuts** (Ctrl + C/V/X/Z/A, etc.) work flawlessly with Devanagari Unicode; they handle matras, ligatures, and halants automatically.  
- **Arrow keys, Home/End, and Page navigation** treat each Hindi grapheme cluster as a single unit, preventing accidental splitting of conjuncts.  
- **Language toggling** via **Alt + Shift** or **Win + Space** (Windows) and **Control + Space** (macOS) lets you switch instantly between Hindi and English, avoiding garbled text.  
- **Formatting shortcuts** (Bold, Italic, Underline, Alignments, Indent) apply to selected Hindi text just as they do for Latin script, and style shortcuts (Alt + Ctrl + 1/2/0) enforce consistent document design.  
- **Practice** through a focused mini‑exercise consolidates the workflow: copy, switch language, format, navigate, undo, and save—all without touching the mouse.  
- **Troubleshooting** common hiccups (read‑only mode, partial selection, language indicator issues) ensures you stay productive.  
- **Cross‑platform parity**: macOS uses Command instead of Control, but the shortcut logic stays identical, enabling seamless typing on any OS.  

Mastering these shortcuts turns Hindi typing from a manual, eye‑straining task into a fluid, efficient process—setting the stage for the advanced character work covered in the next modules.

modules.title: Module 7: Typing Special Characters, Numerals, and Punctuation
modules.content:
## When Numbers Meet Poetry: A Real‑World Typing Challenge  

Imagine you are drafting a short Hindi news piece for a local newspaper:

> **“भारत ने 2024‑में ७५ % की आर्थिक वृद्धि हासिल की।”**  
>  
> **“सूर्य — संध्या, २ जनवरी को, ०१:३० बजे, नई सड़क का उद्घाटन।”**  

The paragraph must display Devanagari digits (०‑९), proper sentence‑ending danda (।), double danda (॥) for a quoted verse, and a variety of punctuation marks—quotation marks, commas, hyphens, and brackets—while preserving the fluid look of complex conjuncts such as **क्ष** and **ज्ञ**.  

If you can type this cleanly and quickly, you’ve mastered the core skill set of Module 7. The sections that follow break down each element, show you the exact keystrokes for both Inscript and popular phonetic layouts, and give you a workflow that ties back to the speed‑building techniques from **Module 5** and the shortcut principles from **Module 6**.

---

## Hindi Numerals (Devanagari Digits)

### 1. Why Use Hindi Digits?  

* **Cultural consistency** – Official documents, school textbooks, and most Hindi‑language publications prefer Devanagari digits.  
* **Readability** – When Hindi text surrounds the number, readers expect the same script for a seamless visual flow.  

You may still need Arabic numerals (0‑9) for technical data, URLs, or when mixing languages. The key is to **choose the script that matches the surrounding text**.

### 2. Typing Devanagari Digits on the Inscript Layout  

| Devanagari Digit | Inscript Key (Shift + ?) | Phonetic Shortcut |
|------------------|--------------------------|-------------------|
| ० (zero)         | `Shift + 0` (top row)    | Type `0` (auto‑maps) |
| १ (one)          | `Shift + 1`              | Type `1` |
| २ (two)          | `Shift + 2`              | Type `2` |
| ३ (three)        | `Shift + 3`              | Type `3` |
| ४ (four)         | `Shift + 4`              | Type `4` |
| ५ (five)         | `Shift + 5`              | Type `5` |
| ६ (six)          | `Shift + 6`              | Type `6` |
| ७ (seven)        | `Shift + 7`              | Type `7` |
| ८ (eight)        | `Shift + 8`              | Type `8` |
| ९ (nine)         | `Shift + 9`              | Type `9` |

> **Tip (Module 5):** Keep the **Shift** finger anchored on the left side of the keyboard while your right hand handles the number keys. This minimizes hand travel and improves speed.

### 3. Switching Between Hindi and Arabic Numerals  

Most Hindi input methods allow you to toggle the numeral style on the fly:

| Input Method | Toggle Command | Result |
|--------------|----------------|--------|
| **Inscript** | `Ctrl + Alt + N` (customizable) | Switches between Devanagari and Arabic digits |
| **Phonetic (Google Indic Keyboard)** | `Ctrl + Shift + N` | Same effect |
| **Windows 10 Hindi Language Bar** | Click the **digit icon** in the language bar | Manual selection |

Remember to **reset the toggle** after finishing a numeric block to avoid accidental mixing.

### 4. Quick Practice  

Type the following sequence, alternating scripts every three digits:

```
०१२ 123 ३४५ 456 ६७८ 789
```

Check that the first, third, and fifth groups use Devanagari digits, while the others stay Arabic.

---

## Danda (।) and Double Danda (॥)

### 1. What They Represent  

* **Danda (।)** – Marks the end of a sentence in Devanagari, equivalent to the period (.) in Latin scripts.  
* **Double Danda (॥)** – Separates verses in poetry or sections in legal documents, similar to a paragraph break.

### 2. Keystrokes for Danda and Double Danda  

| Symbol | Inscript | Phonetic | Shortcut (Module 6) |
|--------|----------|----------|---------------------|
| Danda (।) | `Shift + वै` (right‑most key on the top row) | Type `.` (dot) while Hindi mode is active | `Alt + .` (commonly works) |
| Double Danda (॥) | `Shift + Shift + वै` (press the same key twice) | Type `..` (two dots) quickly | `Alt + Shift + .` |

> **Note:** On many phonetic keyboards, the simple period `.` automatically produces a danda when Hindi mode is on. Press it twice for a double danda.

### 3. When to Use Each  

| Context | Preferred Symbol |
|---------|-----------------|
| Ordinary prose, news article | Danda (।) |
| Poetry, shloka, legal clauses | Double Danda (॥) |
| Mixed English‑Hindi sentences (e.g., “The report was released on 12 जनवरी।” ) | Danda (।) – keep the script‑consistent punctuation |

### 4. Common Pitfall  

* Accidentally typing a Latin period after a Hindi sentence leads to **visual inconsistency** and can confuse screen‑readers. Always verify that the final punctuation is a danda, not a period.

### 5. Speed Drill (Module 5)  

Set a timer for 30 seconds and type the following 10 sentences, each ending with a danda:

```
पहला चरण पूरा हो गया। 
दूसरा चरण शुरू किया गया। 
तीसरा चरण सफल रहा। 
```

Aim for **no pauses** between the last word and the danda. This builds the reflex of reaching for the danda key as the natural sentence terminator.

---

## Punctuation in Hindi Text

Hindi uses many of the same punctuation marks as English, but the **Unicode code points** differ. Below is a quick reference for the most frequently used symbols, with their keystrokes for both Inscript and phonetic layouts.

### 1. Quotation Marks  

| Symbol | Name | Inscript | Phonetic | Use in Hindi |
|--------|------|----------|----------|--------------|
| “ ”   | Double “smart” quotes | `Shift + 2` (produces “) then `Shift + 2` again for ” | Type `"` (double‑quote) – auto‑converts | Enclose direct speech or citations |
| ‘ ’   | Single “smart” quotes | `Shift + 3` (produces ‘) then `Shift + 3` again for ’ | Type `'` (apostrophe) – auto‑converts | For nested quotations |
